title: KV fragmentation and page-boundary benchmarking (draft)
content:
Goal:
- Quick hypothesize-and-test doc: whether page alignment / fragmentation of the KV residency store is a first-class contributor to tail latency and throughput loss under realistic chat workloads.
- Produce actionable mitigations (hugepages, allocator tweaks, eviction region compaction) so SRE can do canary.

Background / why I care:
- We see p99 latency spikes and throughput drops when hotset growth crosses certain sizes during high-concurrency chat tests.
- Traditional KV metrics (hit rate, occupancy) don't explain spikes: hit rate stays ~90% while p99 doubles.
- Hypothesis: when the working set straddles page boundaries, we observe extra page-table churn, TLB pressure and DMA/cache line scattering that increases memory bandwidth and stalls on repeated page flips (soft fault-like behavior at process level).

Testbed (hardware & env):
- Instance: g4dn.12xlarge-like node (48 vCPU, 384 GiB RAM), NVMe-backed serving.
- Kernel: Ubuntu 22.04, 5.15.x.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime commit 4f3a7b (kv-resident v2), jemalloc default.
- Hugepages: tests run both with hugepages disabled and enabled (2MB hugetlbfs).
- NUMA: single-socket slice for baseline, and a cross-node NUMA run to verify no cross-node interleaving artifacts.

Workload (micro + integrated):
1) Micro: synthetic KV loader that writes keys sized to vary alignment: 48B, 128B, 1KB, 3KB, 8KB, 12KB. Keys inserted to create contiguous and deliberately fragmented allocations.
2) Integrated: synthetic chat workload based on prod trace sampling (50K requests over 10 minutes), request sizes ~average 600 tokens, concurrency 64.

Metrics collected:
- Token/sec (throughput), latency p50/p95/p99 (ms) from runtime traces.
- KV hit/reuse rates from counters.
- perf counters: LLC-load-misses, dTLB-load-misses, cycles, instructions, mem_uops_retired.all_loads
- /proc/vmstat counters: pgfaults, pgmajfaults, pgsteal (where applicable)
- sar / perf mem for bandwidth (MB/s read/write)

Commands used (quick reference):
- perf stat -e cache-misses,cycles,branch-misses,dTLB-load-misses -p <pid> -I 1000
- perf mem record -e mem_load_uops_retired.l1_miss -p <pid> -- sleep 60
- numactl --physcpubind=0-23 --membind=0 ./kv-bench --keys=1M --pattern=fragmented
- cat /proc/vmstat before/after run

Experiment 1: page-alignment sweep (micro)
- Method: allocate keys with varying size/alignment, measure reuse and page boundary crossing ratio (computed post-hoc by analyzing allocation offsets).
- Result summary (median of 3 runs, concurrency 16):
  * Aligned allocations (sizes multiple of 4096): throughput baseline 100% (reference).
  * Misaligned allocations (random start offsets within page): throughput -12% p50, p99 +40% and LLC-load-misses +22%
  * Keys that straddle two pages (size ~1.5x page): worst: throughput -28%, p99 +85%

Interpretation:
- When many hot keys straddle page boundaries, evictions and re-warm cause additional cache/TLB churn; repeated small accesses trigger more memory reads per logical key.
- dTLB-load-misses correlate strongly with p99 spikes (Spearman rho ~0.72 across runs).

Experiment 2: fragmentation density vs eviction churn (integrated)
- Method: vary how compact the KV arena is (controlled by background compaction runs) and measure eviction writebacks and reuse rate.
- Observations:
  * High fragmentation (simulated by random-sized key churn) increases eviction rate by ~35% and reduces reuse by ~18%.
  * Memory bandwidth (read) increases by ~15% under the same load; write bandwidth also increases during eviction bursts.
  * p99 latency aligned to eviction bursts.

Experiment 3: hugepages toggle
- With 2MB hugepages enabled and arenas built on hugetlbfs:
  * dTLB misses drop significantly for large contiguous hotsets, p99 improves by ~20%.
  * For very fragmented allocations (many small keys), hugepages sometimes worsen throughput (~5%) because internal fragmentation increases and we end up scanning larger pages for small hot entries.

Perf trace anecdote (single interesting trace):
- During a p99 spike we observed repeated sequences: llc-load-miss -> dTLB-load-miss -> mem_load_uops_retired.stlb_miss -> service stall. The sequence repeated ~1200x in a 30s window for the same request group.

Hypotheses refined:
1) Page-boundary crossing of frequently accessed keys creates disproportionate TLB/LLC noise, worsening tail latency.
2) Eviction policies that are unaware of page locality can cause thrashing: evicting keys across many pages increases page cache pressure and bandwidth.
3) Large pages help when hotset is compacted; they hurt when hotset is highly fragmented.

Immediate mitigations to try (ranked):
- Short term (low-risk): enable jemalloc aggressive coalescing for arenas that back KV residency; bump arena size to prefer contiguous runs for hot keys.
- Mid term: page-aware eviction policy: prioritize evictions inside pages that reduce the number of partially-filled pages (compact hot pages first).
- Mid term: region compaction background worker that migrates hot keys into contiguous page ranges during low load.
- Ops knob: enable hugepages for dedicated nodes where workloads have large contiguous hotsets (add to Dedicated config).
- Experimental: per-key allocator metadata storing page-offset to bias allocations to page-aligned boundaries for frequently-hot keys.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Quantify memory overhead of region compaction (copy cost) vs p99 reduction. Add a cost model.
- Should eviction policy be page-first or locality-first? Build a micro-sim to answer.
- Verify behavior on different kernel versions and on arm64 instances (Milan) — TLB sizes differ.
- Check interaction with caching layers (prefix caching) and streaming responses.

Next experiments planned:
1) Nightly canary: run hugepages vs no-hugepages on Dedicated pool for 2 hours with production trace sample. Capture bandwidth, p99, eviction cycles.
2) Implement a simple page-aware eviction prototype (C++ ~200 LOC) that prefers evicting items to reduce number of partially-filled pages; compare to LRU baseline on same trace.
3) Run jemalloc vs mimalloc vs tcmalloc for allocation patterns — collect fragmentation vs throughput.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; data tables attached as artifacts in the linked PR (perf traces and CSVs).
- If you have a preference for a quick/cheap mitigation I can prioritize jemalloc config and hugepages canary; region compaction will require more design + correctness review.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Page-boundary fragmentation appears to explain a sizeable part of tail latency and extra memory bandwidth under heavy KV churn.
- Hugepages help for compact hotsets but can hurt fragmented workloads.
- Best path: short-term allocator/jemalloc tweaks + mid-term page-aware eviction and optional compaction background worker.

Raw numbers appendix (representative):
- Baseline (aligned): throughput 18.2k tokens/s, p99 220ms, LLC-miss 1.2M/min, dTLB-miss 48k/min
- Misaligned heavy-straddle: throughput 13.1k tokens/s (-28%), p99 409ms (+86%), LLC-miss 1.6M/min, dTLB-miss 88k/min
- Hugepages-on (compact hotset): throughput 20.6k tokens/s (+13%), p99 175ms (-20%)
